title: Indian Americans Mark America's 250th Anniversary With Flag Ceremonies, Naval Heritage, and a Look at Their Own Story
excerpt: From BAPS temples illuminated in red, white, and blue to an Indian Navy vessel sailing into Boston Harbor, the community celebrated while reflecting on its journey.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • INS Sudarshini represented India at Sail Boston 250, celebrating America's 250th anniversary.
  • BAPS temples across the US hosted flag ceremonies, honoring veterans and illuminating in national colors.
  • PM Modi congratulated Trump and the American people on the anniversary, emphasizing shared values.
  • NYC Mayor Mamdani highlighted the importance of immigrant contributions to American democracy.
  • The Indian American community, now 4.8 million, plays a vital role in technology and entrepreneurship.

Sail Boston 250 event details

An Indian Navy Ship in Boston Harbor

Indian Naval Ship Sudarshini sailed into Boston Harbor as part of Sail Boston 250, joining an international fleet of tall ships and military vessels gathered to mark the 250th anniversary of American independence. The ship entered the historic port flying the Indian tricolour in the Parade of Sails, with India's Consul General in Boston, Raghuram S., embarking at sea to take a firsthand account of the voyage.

The Consulate General of India in Boston described the participation as "underscoring India's rich maritime heritage and maritime cooperation between India and the US." Boston was the final stop on the Sail 250 tour, following port calls in New Orleans, Norfolk, Baltimore, and New York City during Independence Day celebrations. Organisers expected more than four million attendees across the events.

![Mayor Mamdani. NYC Mayor Mamdani highlighted the importance of immigrant contributions to American democracy.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/Zohran_Mamdani_05.25.25_%28b%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/3840px-Zohran_Mamdani_05.25.25_%28b%29_%28cropped%29.jpg)

Temples Lit in Red, White, and Blue

BAPS Swaminarayan Sanstha organised celebrations across its mandirs in the United States. At the Akshardham complex in Robbinsville, New Jersey, thousands of community members waved American flags during a ceremony honouring faith, service, and civic pride. Veterans participated in the flag-hoisting ceremony alongside families and devotees.

In Los Angeles, the BAPS mandir held a flag-raising ceremony with local veterans and opened its doors to the broader community. In Houston, mayors from four cities — Sugar Land, Missouri City, Pearland, and Stafford — joined as the mandir was illuminated in the national colours and the anthem played.

Many celebrations highlighted religious freedom and pluralism. His Holiness Mahant Swami Maharaj offered a special letter with prayers for America, noting that "the freedoms and opportunities of this nation have allowed our community to become part of the American story."

From Exclusion to Influence

The anniversary prompted reflection on the Indian American community's arc. The Indian Eye published a timeline spanning from the earliest Indian arrivals — farmers who faced racial exclusion acts in the early 1900s — to Kamala Harris's swearing-in as the first Indian American Vice President in 2021.

"Our shared belief in democracy, rule of law and the limitless potential of our people make our friendship a force for global good."

— PM Narendra Modi, on X

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, himself of Indian origin, used his anniversary address to celebrate the nation's immigrant heritage. He described the United States as an ongoing "grand experiment in self-governance" that continues to evolve through the contributions of successive generations.

PM Modi extended congratulations to Trump and the American people. Trump reshared the message on Truth Social. US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor thanked the Prime Minister for the wishes.

What's Next

The White House has said the 250th anniversary celebrations, which began on Memorial Day 2025, will continue through the end of 2026, engaging government, the private sector, and educational institutions nationwide. For the Indian American community, the milestone offered a chance to publicly claim their place in the American story — a community now 4.8 million strong that contributes disproportionately to the nation's technology, medical, and entrepreneurial sectors.
